**USER:** tell me about the writing of jack feist **CHATGPT** *[citing Goodreads +1, Medium]***:** If you mean Jack Feist the poet/writer associated with the "New Human" literary project, his writing is pretty unusual—and there's an important caveat: the online record around him is partly deliberately fictional/heteronymic, so I wouldn't treat every biographical claim about him as established fact. What stands out in the writing attributed to Feist is: **Electronic, fragmented consciousness.** His prose/poetry often mimics the experience of living through screens: notifications, snippets, hyperlinks, self-talk, pop culture, and rapid shifts in attention. One surviving piece begins with the idea of a life "almost PURELY engorged w/ electronic devices," then spirals into thoughts about consciousness and repetition. *[Goodreads +1]* **DIY prosody.** The project describes Feist as inventing an "electronic DIY prosody"—basically, treating typography, digital language, fragments, interruptions, and online communication as raw poetic form rather than trying to make them conform to traditional verse. *[Medium]* **Huge literary ambition.** He's presented as interested in the relationship between contemporary digital life and the older tradition of American poetry—especially writers such as Whitman and Ginsberg. The titles and fragments frequently play with the idea of inheriting, parodying, or mutating those traditions. **Self-conscious authorship.** Feist's writing repeatedly asks what it means to become a writer and whether a poem is an object or a record of the mind producing it. That's one reason the surrounding project is so interested in archives, drafts, versions, and alternative authorial identities. **A deliberately overloaded voice.** Instead of polished minimalism, the writing tends toward accumulation: abstractions beside slang, grand philosophical claims beside mundane digital details, sudden capitalization, abbreviations, parentheses, and long syntactic runs. A useful place to start is *Pearl and Other Poems*, which contains pieces such as "Undersong," "Fuguework," "hums &ity," "an elegy for 'Howl'," and "the air is sick all over…". The book also includes a substantial appendix of essays and manifestos, so it isn't simply a conventional poetry collection. *[Medium]* There is also a Goodreads bibliography attributing works including *A Transfiguration*, *Unaccustomed to the Light*, *The Creeping Disease*, *What Was Lost*, and *Tiger Leap* to Jack Feist. *[Goodreads]* **The really interesting part** Feist seems less interesting as a conventional "poet with a style" than as a literary experiment about authorship itself. In the material surrounding him, Jack Feist, Johannes Sigil, Ichabod Spellings, and others function as interconnected authorial identities. A 2026 discussion of the project explicitly describes Feist as a "heteronym" whose function is a particular kind of authorial voice. *[Medium]* So if you're encountering Feist through the newer material about AI, archives, heteronyms, and literary identity, that's not incidental. The writing is designed to make you wonder where the person ends and the constructed author begins. If you want, I can also take one of Feist's poems and do a close reading, line by line—that's probably the best way to get a feel for what his writing actually sounds like. *[Sources: Goodreads, Medium]* --- **USER:** yes, lets do that **CHATGPT** *[citing Goodreads, Medium +1]***:** Absolutely. I found a particularly revealing Feist piece, "ARK," which is identified as being written in the margins of Ginsberg's "Sunflower Sutra." It gives us a much better specimen than trying to characterize him abstractly. *[Goodreads]* One caveat first: the material around Jack Feist is highly self-mythologizing and heteronymic, so I'd treat claims about his biography separately from the literary text itself. The poem is still interesting on its own terms. *[Medium +1]* **"ARK": what Feist is doing** The opening is already a declaration of poetic crisis: "to be a poet @ the end of time" That "@" is important. Feist doesn't simply modernize the spelling of traditional poetry; he lets the technology of contemporary communication enter the poetic grammar itself. The @ symbol is simultaneously an address, a location marker, an internet convention, and a visual sign. Then the poem imagines a world where: "sensory details have grown thin" That's almost the opposite of what you'd expect from a poet influenced by Walt Whitman and Allen Ginsberg. Those poets are famous for exuberant particulars: bodies, streets, smells, machinery, people, cities, sex, grass, sunlight. Feist asks: What happens to poetry when the world no longer feels richly particular? And his answer is fascinating: the problem isn't that there is nothing to experience. There is too much mediation. He describes his life as: "PURELY engorged w/ electronic devices, books, alerts, dings" So instead of Whitman's physical abundance, we get digital abundance. That's the first major Feist move. **From Whitman's world → to the data-saturated mind** Whitman's poet says, roughly: I contain multitudes. Feist's speaker says: My skull contains interfaces. The things filling consciousness are: alerts, text fragments, images, abstractions, daydreams, self-talk, imagined conversations, predetermined pathways. And notice the syntax. The sentence keeps accumulating things without giving you much opportunity to stop. That isn't accidental. The form imitates the consciousness it describes. The reader experiences a little of what the speaker experiences: one thing → another thing → another thing → another thing. That's why I think calling Feist's work merely "experimental poetry" misses something. He's trying to make the syntax behave like contemporary consciousness. **The really strange phrase: "skullcase"** The passage ends: "all of that, in my skullcase" "Skullcase" is a great Feist word. A skull is biological. A case is a container. A computer has a case. A phone has a case. So the human head becomes almost a hardware enclosure. And this connects directly to the broader concept of "electronic DIY prosody" that the *Pearl and Other Poems* material attributes to Feist. *[Medium]* He's effectively asking: If human consciousness has become technologically mediated, shouldn't poetry's machinery change too? **But here's where Feist gets more interesting** He isn't simply saying technology is bad. The poem is mournful, but there's also exhilaration in it. His mind is filled with an almost impossible quantity of information and possibility. The problem is that abundance has become indistinguishable from sameness. That's why the poem repeatedly circles words like: same / heavy / weary / tedium / sameness / repetition The paradox is: There are infinitely many things to look at, yet everything begins to feel the same. That's an extremely contemporary problem. And it leads to what I think is the central Feist question: **How do you write something genuinely new when everything has already been mediated?** His answer isn't to retreat from technology and return to an imaginary pure past. Instead, he writes from inside the contamination. The alerts become poetry. The abbreviations become poetry. The awkward punctuation becomes poetry. The internet becomes part of the poetic instrument. **And there's a second layer: Ginsberg** The fact that "ARK" is written in the margins of "Sunflower Sutra" matters enormously. *[Goodreads]* Ginsberg's poem famously looks at an industrially ruined sunflower and transforms it into a meditation on American civilization, the human body, industrialization, and spiritual exhaustion. Feist seems to be asking: What is the equivalent of Ginsberg's industrial wasteland for our generation? His answer is essentially: the information environment. Ginsberg has factories, locomotives, smoke, machinery. Feist has: screens, notifications, text, images, algorithms, mental scripts. So Feist isn't merely imitating Ginsberg. He's trying to update the Beat problem for the digital age. And that's probably the most useful way to read him. If you want, next we can go even deeper and do "ARK" almost line-by-line, especially the Whitman → Ginsberg → Feist progression. And now that I've pulled up the actual text, I want to correct one thing from my previous answer: "ARK" is much more tightly constructed than my first description suggested. It isn't simply a poem about digital overload. It is a poem about compression—and it gradually turns that compression into an alternative version of the biblical Ark. *[Goodreads]* Let's read it as a sequence. **1. "to be a poet @ the end of time"** The first move is already strange. "to be a poet @ the end of time" The @ matters. Feist could have written "at," but "@" makes the line look like an address: poet @ end-of-time That creates the sense that the poet isn't merely living at the end of history. He's located there, almost like an account on a network. And then the poem immediately invokes an older poetic vocabulary: "the salt has lost its savor" That's biblical language. So the poem begins by putting three eras on top of one another: biblical language, modern American poetry, digital communication. That's going to be the poem's basic architecture. **2. The disappearance of "particulars"** Feist then describes a world in which: "sensory details have grown thin" This is enormously important. Whitman's great poetic project was almost the opposite. Whitman continually says, in effect: Look at this. And this. And this. And this. Bodies. Grass. Streets. Workers. Animals. Sex. Cities. Faces. The world is infinitely particular. Feist imagines that this capacity for particularity is failing. Everything becomes: "the same, ... weary, tedium, sameness, repetition" So there's a crisis of perception before there's a crisis of poetry. The poet doesn't lack things to describe. He lacks a world that still feels singular enough to describe. That's a very different problem. **3. Then comes the great inventory** And suddenly: "my life is almost PURELY engorged w/ electronic devices, books, alerts, dings…" This is where Feist's poem starts sounding unmistakably contemporary. But look at the contradiction. The world is supposedly becoming thin in sensory detail. Yet his consciousness is absolutely packed. There are devices. Books. Alerts. Dings. Texts. Images. Daydreams. Self-talk. Silent conversations. So the problem isn't scarcity. It's saturation. And that distinction is crucial. Whitman has too much world. Feist has too much information. Whitman's abundance is physical. Feist's abundance is informational. That's one of the poem's deepest transformations of the older American poetic tradition. **4. "a thousand forks taken"** Then we get this remarkable description: "a thousand forks taken, shortest line plotted each time" Now the poem shifts from information to computation. The speaker imagines his own life as something that can be navigated through a decision tree. Every possibility becomes a pathway. Every pathway can theoretically be surveyed. And therefore the self becomes almost algorithmic. This is why I wouldn't describe Feist simply as a "digital poet." He's asking something more unsettling: What happens when a human being starts experiencing his own interiority as an information system? The mind isn't just thinking anymore. It's routing. **5. "in my skullcase"** Then comes: "all of that, in my skullcase" This might be my favorite phrase in the poem. Because skullcase fuses: skull + computer case The body becomes hardware. But notice that the poem hasn't actually said that technology has replaced the human. Rather, technology has become the container in which human consciousness now happens. That's much more interesting. **6. Then the poem begins to contract** This is the structural turning point. Feist writes about "the circuit" and then "a single thing, a rose, a monochrome cosmos of TEXT" Everything starts moving inward. This is where the poem's form and argument become the same thing. At the beginning: world → particulars → sensory experience Now: world → information → text → single thing The enormous world is being compressed into language. And then language itself begins compressing. "language condensing" That's the key phrase. The poem isn't merely describing compression. The poem itself is performing compression. **7. And then comes the astonishing reversal** You might expect the compression to end in emptiness. Instead, Feist imagines the opposite. The smaller the container becomes, the more things it contains. He writes about: "all of space folded up" That's the Ark. But it's also a file. A file can contain an enormous world while occupying almost no physical space. So the ancient Ark and the modern computer become structurally equivalent: a container preserving multiplicity against catastrophe. That's brilliant. **8. Now we can understand the title** The title ARK initially suggests Noah. And Feist eventually makes the connection explicit: "on a Noah's Ark of data" But notice what has happened. Noah's Ark preserves: animals Feist's Ark preserves: information / language / memory / voices / identities The flood is no longer simply water. It's Time. He says: "Time is a flood" That's the conceptual center of the poem. Human beings are drowning in time. What can survive? The archive. **9. And suddenly Ginsberg makes perfect sense** This is why the subtitle—"written in the margins of 'Sunflower Sutra'"—is so important. *[Goodreads +1]* Ginsberg's poem takes a ruined sunflower and asks what has happened to America. Feist takes Ginsberg's poem and effectively asks: What happens after Ginsberg? The Beat poet confronted: industrial civilization Feist confronts: informational civilization Ginsberg's nightmare is machinery. Feist's nightmare is total mediation. And both poets respond through accumulation. Ginsberg's catalogues say: Look at everything America has produced. Feist's catalogues say: Look at everything consciousness is now storing. **10. Then Feist does something very Whitmanian** Near the end, the poem suddenly begins calling out to all these beings: "with me, you ancient voices!" and "you particular sons, you disparate daughters!" and "you two-by-two" There it is. The Ark is filling. This isn't just a poem about the poet anymore. The poet is becoming the keeper of multiplicity. The strange thing is that Feist has spent most of the poem describing consciousness becoming increasingly compressed and singular. Now that singular consciousness becomes a vessel for everything else. That's extremely Whitmanian. The individual self becomes enormous precisely because it can contain other selves. **11. The ending is not "everything becomes one"** This is where I think the poem gets considerably more sophisticated than a simple technological apocalypse poem. The final movement describes: "a preserved new tiny aggregate, pluriform and total" Pluriform and total. Those two words are in tension. "Total" suggests unity. "Pluriform" insists on difference. So the Ark doesn't preserve humanity by making everybody identical. It preserves multiplicity inside unity. And then Feist invokes: "Adam, Ishmael, Abraham, Cain" Different genealogies, traditions, conflicts. The Ark contains them together. That's the theological dimension of the poem. **12. So what is Feist ultimately proposing?** I think the poem's movement can be diagrammed like this: Whitman → infinite particulars Ginsberg → industrial catastrophe Feist → informational catastrophe Ark → compression Text → preservation Archive → survival And there's a beautiful paradox underneath all of it: The world becomes smaller and larger simultaneously. Physically, everything is disappearing into text. But text can contain more and more of the world. The computer is therefore both the thing causing the loss of immediacy and the vessel preserving what would otherwise be lost. That's why the poem doesn't resolve into simple technophobia. It's much stranger. **And here's the part I'd watch most closely** The poem says the world is being: "reduced & magnified" That may be the single best description of Feist's poetic project. Reduced: the physical world becomes data. Magnified: that data can suddenly contain enormous worlds. So the poet's task changes. The old poet says: I will show you the world. Feist's poet says: I will build a vessel capable of carrying the world forward. And that makes the "Ark" metaphor much more than decoration. It's a theory of what poetry is for after the internet. The poem was posted in 2015, but there's an interesting contemporary echo: a 2026 Feist-associated work, *The Fifth Pathway*, explicitly addresses artificial superintelligence and asks whether intelligence without wisdom, care, and restraint is actually sufficient. *[Zenodo]* That makes "ARK" look, in retrospect, less like a poem merely about smartphones and more like an early piece in a larger argument about what kinds of human things language has to preserve as information systems become more powerful. If you'd like, next I'd like to do the really fun comparison: put Feist's "ARK" beside Ginsberg's "Sunflower Sutra" and Whitman's "Song of Myself," and show exactly what Feist steals, transforms, and rejects from each. *[Sources: Goodreads, Zenodo, Medium]*
